prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "ExxonMobil Holdings Corp" (ticker XOM), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "XOM", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation
markets: Carbon capture, lithium and other low-carbon solutions

mission.statement: Create sustainable solutions that improve quality of life and meet society's evolving needs.
mission.source: ExxonMobil corporate website, Who we are page (purpose statement)
mission.plain: ExxonMobil wants to supply the energy and materials people need to live better lives, in ways that can last.

about.plain: ExxonMobil finds oil and natural gas deep underground and under the sea, and pumps it out. It turns that oil into gasoline, diesel and jet fuel in huge refineries, and into plastics and chemicals in big factories. It sells these products all over the world. It is one of the biggest energy companies on Earth.
about.customers: Drivers, airlines, shipping firms, factories, plastics makers and other businesses that need fuel, gas and chemicals.
about.everyday: Exxon and Mobil gas stations and Mobil 1 motor oil are familiar to many drivers.

money.plain: gasoline, diesel and jet fuel from its refineries
crude oil and natural gas, including LNG, from fields like the Permian and Guyana
basic plastics and chemicals such as polyethylene
storing CO2 underground for other companies, plus hydrogen and lithium
Proxxima resins and synthetic graphite for batteries

result.summary: ExxonMobil sells commodities, so it cannot charge more than the market price; its advantage comes from scale, low-cost resources and integration. Its 45% operated stake in Guyana's Stabroek block and its Permian position after buying Pioneer in 2024 give it some of the lowest-cost, fastest-growing barrels in the industry, and its integrated refining and chemical plants capture more value per barrel. That makes it a narrow but real cost-based moat in a cyclical industry.

pricingPower.evidence: Revenue swings with oil and gas prices it does not control: total revenues and other income went from $181,502M in 2020 to $413,680M in 2022 and back to $332,238M in 2025, then jumped to $116,017M in Q2 2026 alone as oil prices spiked.

moats.evidence: Exxon, Esso and Mobil brands and Mobil 1 lubricants carry some premium, but fuel buyers mostly choose on price and location.
Fuel and bulk chemical customers can switch suppliers easily; only some specialty chemical and lubricant grades are specified into customers' products.
More customers do not make its oil or chemicals more valuable to other customers.

Production of 4,736 thousand oil-equivalent barrels a day in 2025, low-cost Guyana and Permian barrels and $15.1 billion of structural cost savings since 2019 (targeting $20 billion by 2030) give it one of the lowest unit costs among the majors.
World-scale integrated sites such as Baytown and Singapore, and LNG projects, need tens of billions of dollars and long lead times, which limits new entrants.
It competes with the same business model as other integrated majors.
Deepwater project execution in Guyana (first oil less than five years after discovery), cube development in the Permian and proprietary catalysts and chemical processes are hard to replicate.
It operates and owns 45% of Guyana's Stabroek block, one of the largest oil discoveries of the past decade, with a fifth FPSO adding 250 thousand barrels a day due to start in 4Q26.

customers.evidence: Mobil 1 and Exxon/Mobil stations have loyal followings, but most of its fuel and chemicals are bought on price under commodity contracts.

talent.evidence: It employs about 61,000 people and recruits top engineers and scientists with strong pay, but oil's declining popularity with young graduates and periodic job cuts weigh on its employer appeal.

product.evidence: Products such as Mobil 1 synthetic oil and its high-performance polymers are well regarded, but fuels and basic chemicals are commodities with little product differentiation.

competitors.name: Chevron Corporation
competitors.note: US integrated major competing in the Permian, LNG, refining and chemicals; now a 30% partner in Guyana's Stabroek block after buying Hess.

competitors.name: Shell plc
competitors.note: Integrated major; leader in LNG trading, deepwater and fuels marketing.

competitors.name: TotalEnergies SE
competitors.note: Integrated major in oil, LNG, refining and chemicals, with a larger power and renewables business.

competitors.name: BP p.l.c.
competitors.note: Integrated major in upstream, refining, fuels retail and trading.

competitors.name: Saudi Arabian Oil Company (Saudi Aramco)
competitors.note: World's largest oil producer, with growing refining and chemicals (SABIC); the lowest-cost barrels.

competitors.name: ConocoPhillips
competitors.note: Largest independent US producer; competes in the Permian, Alaska and LNG.

competitors.name: PetroChina Company Limited
competitors.note: Chinese state-controlled oil, gas and refining giant.

competitors.name: China Petroleum & Chemical Corporation (Sinopec)
competitors.note: Largest refiner and a major petrochemical maker, competing in Asian fuels and chemicals.

competitors.name: Equinor ASA
competitors.note: Norwegian oil and gas producer competing in offshore production and European gas supply.

competitors.name: Petróleo Brasileiro S.A. (Petrobras)
competitors.note: Brazilian deepwater producer competing with Guyana for offshore Atlantic barrels.

competitors.name: Occidental Petroleum Corporation
competitors.note: Permian producer and rival in carbon capture and direct air capture.

competitors.name: Marathon Petroleum Corporation
competitors.note: Largest US refiner, competing in fuels.

competitors.name: Valero Energy Corporation
competitors.note: Large independent refiner competing in US Gulf Coast and export fuels.

competitors.name: Dow Inc.
competitors.note: Competes in polyethylene and other commodity chemicals.

threats: Oil and gas price swings, which drive most of its earnings, and a possible reversal of the 2026 price spike.
Long-term demand decline from electric vehicles, efficiency and climate policy.
Chevron's entry into Guyana's Stabroek block via Hess, and political or border risk around Guyana and Venezuela.
Chinese and Middle Eastern overcapacity in petrochemicals, squeezing chemical margins.
Climate litigation, carbon taxes and methane rules that raise costs or limit projects.
Low-carbon bets (carbon capture, hydrogen, lithium) depend on government subsidies and may not earn adequate returns.

ceo.name: Darren Woods
ceo.background: Electrical engineer (Texas A&M), Kellogg (Northwestern) MBA; joined Exxon in 1992 and ran its refining and chemical businesses before becoming chairman and CEO.

c1.evidence: ExxonMobil leads Western oil majors, but oil and gas is a mature, cyclical industry, not an emerging one.

c2.evidence: Customers buy on price, but its low-cost Guyana and Permian resources and integrated plants are hard to copy and should last for decades.

c3.evidence: Exxon and Mobil are household names and it is the largest US oil company, but few consumers would actively recommend it.

c4.evidence: Its purpose is to create sustainable solutions that improve quality of life, and affordable energy does matter, but management is mainly driven by returns to shareholders.

c6.evidence: “big oil, powerful, polluter”; the impression is mixed to negative with the general public, though investors see it as well run and reliable.

c7.evidence: The oil, gas and chemicals market is enormous but growing slowly, and faces a long-term threat from electrification rather than riding a secular tailwind.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into carbon capture (after buying Denbury in 2023), lithium, Proxxima resins and synthetic graphite, but these are small next to the core business.

m1.evidence: Woods has a clear long-term plan built on Guyana, the Permian and cost cuts, but it extends the existing business rather than imagining a new one.

m2.evidence: Woods is a 30-year company veteran who thinks long term, pursuing multi-decade projects like Guyana, but he is a hired professional rather than a founder.

m4.evidence: He stresses safety and operational excellence, but also led sizable job cuts and restructuring to lower costs.

m5.evidence: Exxon has a strong engineering and research culture that develops new catalysts, materials and processes, but it is conservative and hierarchical.

m6.evidence: Woods is an electrical engineer who spent his career running refining and chemical operations.

m7.evidence: He argues that affordable energy lifts living standards and backs carbon capture, but critics say the company has resisted faster climate action.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Woods giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Woods is a low-key corporate executive without a widely known public persona.

m9.evidence: Under Woods production rose to 4,736 thousand oil-equivalent barrels a day in 2025, he closed the Pioneer and Denbury deals, and Q2 2026 net income reached $14,525M.

m10.evidence: ExxonMobil is known for tight cost control, with $15.1 billion of structural savings since 2019, but not for symbolic frugality.

c10.evidence: Its fuels, gas and plastics are used by billions of people every day for transport, heating, power and everyday goods.

p2.evidence: Drilling deepwater wells off Guyana and running world-scale refineries and chemical plants is extremely hard and supplies energy the world depends on.

f1.evidence: Total revenues and other income fell in 2023 (to $344,582M from $413,680M) and in 2025 (to $332,238M), tracking oil prices.

f2.evidence: Net margin rose from a loss in 2020 to 8.7% in 2025, but it peaked at 13.5% in 2022 and moves with commodity prices rather than steadily.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 debt was $42,368M against $10,588M of cash and $51,970M of 2025 operating cash flow, with debt-to-capital around 14% and positive equity.

f4.evidence: Operating cash flow rose from $14,668M in 2020 to $51,970M in 2025, but it fell from the 2022 peak of $76,797M.

v1.evidence: Gasoline and chemicals are commodities, so an ordinary person has no practical reason to choose Exxon fuel over a rival's.

v2.evidence: ExxonMobil is not typically ranked among the best companies to work for, despite good pay for engineers.

c5.evidence: If ExxonMobil vanished overnight, fuel and plastics prices would jump and supply would be tight until rivals filled the gap, but its products are interchangeable with others'.
